abstract: Motivation Diseases often share underlying molecular characteristics captured by transcriptional responses. Leveraging this knowledge transfer can aid in uncovering novel disease biology and drug repurposing. Large-scale transcriptomic datasets and disease signatures provide an opportunity to computationally identify these shared disease relationships based on shared genome-wide gene expression changes. However, disease signatures are strongly influenced by sample tissue, making it difficult to distinguish shared disease biology from shared tissue origin. Despite this challenge, existing computational approaches do not systematically take into account or evaluate the impact of tissue on their predictions. Results We present SigMatch, a systematic evaluation of the impact of sample tissue on transcriptomic-based disease relationship prioritization. We evaluate this impact on existing correlation- and rank-based methods, and on an alternative family called reconstruction-based methods. In particular, we examine (i) mechanistic disease relationships given the context of sample tissues and (ii) prediction agreement with external evidence of disease relatedness based on shared genes, symptoms, drugs, and comorbidities. We found that predicted disease relationships by all the methods are heavily influenced by sample tissue. Tissue-specific genes are not the sole driver of the prediction scores. Across methods, removal of tissue-specific genes did not reduce the observed tissue-dependent patterns or improve recovery of evidence-supported disease pairs. This work demonstrates substantial sample-tissue influence in transcriptomic similarities between diseases and that sample tissue should be considered when identifying and interpreting inferred transcriptomic disease relationships.
